meta.name: Restaurants
meta._note: SEED for the industry-page spine dev surface (a trade across places). Place-stable margin shape + a like-for-like 'where it pays best' read, plus the subtype drill (the richness lever). Illustrative; wire to industry_margins + the activity board on promotion. The Margin Index is the hero POV.

provenance_line: Illustrative model, not yet wired to measured accounts. Figures are directional and shown so the shape reads true.

verdict.headline: The owner keeps about $7 of every $100 a customer spends: a thin keep, below the all-trades average, won on volume and cost control.
verdict.lead: Of every $100 taken, food and labour swallow two-thirds before rent is paid. The model only works at scale, with a tight kitchen and a rota that bends to the day.
verdict.close: The operators who last are not the best cooks. They are the best at rota, waste and rent.

_meta.source: derived from the money_split $100 stack (the one canonical margin model on this page)

margins._identity: gross 67 = 100 - food 33; operating 22 = 67 - wages 33 - rent 12; net 7 = 22 - other 15. ONE model: ladder = stack = captions.

demand.trend_note: Demand indexed to the pre-dip level (100): the dip was sharp, the climb back steady but not yet complete.
demand.saturation_note: Openings roughly match closings in a mature field, so a new room's covers mostly come from somebody else's tables.
demand.demand_note: Discretionary spend and convenience drive traffic; sensitive to disposable income and local foot traffic.

_meta.source: Most diners spend 11-30 USD per person per visit (mode ~11-20), with dining-out frequency around 5 times a month; developed-market restaurant density is roughly 20-25 outlets per 10k residents. Trend reflects the post-2020 dip then recovery.
_meta.method: Per-head spend, frequency and density each held from 2+ dining and density datasets; trend indexed to the pandemic dip and recovery.

list.name: Fast food / quick service
list.note: Simpler menu and faster turns lift net margin above full-service.

list.name: Fast casual
list.note: Higher checks than QSR with lean labor; margins hold up well.

list.name: Cafe / bistro
list.note: Lower fit-out and beverage-led margins keep it near the baseline.

list.name: Full-service casual dining
list.note: Heavier labor and space drag net margin below the blended average.

list.name: Fine dining
list.note: High ticket but very high labor, ingredient and fit-out cost thin the margin.

subtypes.note: A leaner build and faster turns beat a grand room: the cheapest doors into the trade also keep the most.

money_split.annotation: Wages and rent decide the year; food cost only edits it.
money_split.fixed_note: Rent, rates and other fixed running costs are about $27 of every $100: the nut that must be filled before the owner sees a cent.
money_split.variable_note: Food and hourly wages flex with covers, about $66 of every $100: the lines a tight kitchen and a sharp rota actually move.

cost_structure._identity: breakeven_utilization = fixed 27 / contribution ratio 0.34 (1 - variable 66 per $100) = ~79% of a typical day's takings; fixed_pct/variable_pct are shares of the $93 cost base (27/93, 66/93).
cost_structure.note: Fixed costs are $27 of a typical $100 day, and each sales dollar contributes 34 cents after food and hourly labour; those two numbers set the bar.

_meta.source: Food cost 28-35% and labor 25-35% of revenue, with prime cost (food plus labor) targeted at 55-65%; rent and occupancy add roughly 6-10%.
_meta.method: Food, labor and prime-cost bands held from 2+ restaurant benchmark studies; lines reconciled to the money_split stack (67% gross / 22% operating / 7% net) so every margin statement on the page agrees.

first_year._identity: Timeline anchors: break-even node at week 26 = ramp_to_breakeven_months 6; payback_years 2.8 = payback.payback_months 34 / 12; the year-end node echoes survival.yr1_pct 80.

nodes.label: Break-even
nodes.sub: month 6: the doors pay the costs

first_year.note: Month six is the median crossing, not a promise: the undercapitalised fail inside the months-three-to-nine cash gap, before the model can prove itself.

_meta.source: Small independents commonly reach cash breakeven within several months to a year, with capital payback often two to three years given high fit-out cost.
_meta.method: Modeled from restaurant startup and payback benchmarks; wide by concept, so mid-point taken.
payback = capital / the owner's annual take: $150K / about $53K a year = ~34 months (2.8 years); gearing at 60% LTV stretches it to 46.

payback.gearing_note: Borrow six of every ten dollars of the fit-out and debt service skims about three points off the keep until the loan clears, so a 7% keep runs nearer 4% and payback slips from 34 months to 46.
payback.note: A typical fit-out pays back in under three years if the room fills; a slow first winter pushes it past four.

cost_drivers.name: Wages
cost_drivers.note: The largest controllable line; rota to demand or it eats the margin.

cost_drivers.name: Rent & rates
cost_drivers.note: Fixed and unforgiving; the address sets the floor under your whole model.

cost_drivers.name: Food cost
cost_drivers.note: Menu engineering and waste move the gross line more than prices do.

suits: Hands-on operators who will work the floor and the rota, not absentee owners.
People who already know hospitality margins and read a P&L weekly.
Anyone who can sign a long lease and survive a slow first winter on reserves.
think_twice: Passion cooks chasing a dream menu over covers-per-night maths.
First-timers expecting passive income; this is a job before it is an asset.
Anyone undercapitalised: the cash gap in months three to nine kills most.

myths: The 90% first-year failure claim is a myth; roughly four in five survive year one.
High gross margin is misleading; labor and rent consume most of it, leaving low single-digit net.
Full tables do not guarantee profit; prime cost creeping above 65% wipes out the margin.
caveats.honest_take: Survival is better than folklore suggests, but the margin is so thin that food and labor cost control, not popularity, decides who makes money.

_meta.source: Recurring themes across restaurant benchmark and survival studies: prime-cost control and the debunked failure myth.
_meta.method: Synthesized from multiple restaurant sources into plain myth-busting lines.

survival.note: The attrition is front-loaded: the rooms that clear the first two winters tend to stay.

_meta.source: About 80% of restaurants survive year one and roughly half reach year five; the often-quoted 90% first-year failure figure is a myth with no data behind it.
_meta.method: Held from 2+ restaurant survival datasets; a 2025 near-zero first-year-failure reading was treated as an anomaly and not used.

seasonality._identity: months[] indexed to an average month = 100, Jan through Dec; low 90 (January) to high 108 (December) = the 20% winter-to-peak swing_pct ((108 - 90) / 90).
seasonality.peak_note: bookings and parties; the quarter that carries the year.
seasonality.trough_note: the post-holiday lull; the cash test of the year.
seasonality.note: Summer travel and December holidays lift sales; post-holiday January and February are the low point.

_meta.source: Sales spike in summer and around the December holidays and slow in January and February; a commonly cited swing is around 19% between winter low and summer high.
_meta.method: Peak and trough months held from 2+ seasonality sources; swing_pct held near the ~19% figure and rounded.

_meta.source: modeled owner take-home, converted to USD, same tax-aware method; directional

where_pays.note: Owner take-home, like-for-like and converted to one currency. A low-rent format rescues the high-rent cities, a rent-heavy one punishes them; the two clear leaders hold.

_meta.source: illustrative keep-per-$100 across neighbouring trades; modeled, not measured

benchmark.avg_note: The broad all-trades average sits near $12 kept per $100, across every trade in the atlas, not just the food ones below.
benchmark.note: Cafes, bars, takeaways and catering each keep more per $100; against the whole trade universe the gap is wider still.

trades.name: Restaurants
trades.why: You are here: thinnest keep of the food trades, won back only on volume.

trades.name: Cafe
trades.why: Coffee carries a fat gross margin that food service never sees.

trades.name: Bar / pub
trades.why: Drink markup and lower food waste lift the keep above the kitchen trades.

trades.name: Takeaway
trades.why: No dining room to staff or seat; rent and labour both run lighter.

trades.name: Catering
trades.why: Covers are booked and paid ahead, so waste and empty-seat risk nearly vanish.

margin_ladder._identity: Mirrors margins (the ONE canonical set, derived from money_split): gross 67 / operating 22 / net 7. Never let this drift from margins.

_meta.source: Gross (after food and beverage cost) typically 65-70%; net runs 3-5% full-service and 6-9% limited-service, blending near 7. Anchor retained.
_meta.method: Anchored inside the held ranges for a blended small independent, then reconciled to the money_split stack so ladder, stack and captions state one model.

sale_exit.buyers_note: Single-location independents sell on SDE; a transferable manager, strong lease and stable sales lift the price and can shift the deal to an EBITDA basis.

_meta.source: Independent single-location restaurants transact around 1.5-3x SDE (avg ~2.1-2.9x); larger multi-unit operations move to 3-5x EBITDA.
_meta.method: Held from 2+ restaurant valuation datasets reporting SDE multiples.
